title: Why can an older search replace the latest result?
answer: An older search can finish last, and an unguarded handler publishes whatever finishes last

checks.question: The user types “ca”, then “cat”, then “ca” again, starting requests with tickets 1, 2 and 3. Request 3 finishes first; request 1 finishes last. Should request 1 be published because its query text matches the current input?
checks.answer: No. The current request is ticket 3. Ticket 1 is an older request even though its text is also “ca”; it may contain older data. Compare request tickets, not query strings, and leave request 3’s result on the page.

checks.question: Suppose the newest request fails, then an older successful request arrives. Does the ticket guard publish the older result as a fallback?
checks.answer: No. Its ticket is still stale. The guard enforces which request may publish; it does not choose a fallback or handle the newest request’s error. An application needs an explicit error or fallback policy.

cases.name: Which search answers first: “cat” answers first

steps.title: Type “ca”, then “cat”: two searches race
steps.line: Predict: “cat” answers first and “ca” last. Which results does the page end on?
steps.caption: Each keystroke starts a search, so “ca” starts first and “cat” second, and the user now wants “cat”. The requests can finish in a different order from the one they started in; here “cat” finishes first. Both requests succeed in this example. The page starts empty and publishes results as they arrive.
steps.picture: Search. Starts. Answers. “ca”. 1st. 2nd. “cat”. 2nd. 1st. The user wants “cat”.

steps.title: Answer: “ca”. The older search lands last and replaces “cat”
steps.line: Predict: what could tell the handler that “ca” is out of date?
steps.caption: An older search can finish last, and an unguarded handler publishes whatever finishes last. “cat” lands first and the page shows it; then “ca” lands and replaces it. The user typed “cat” and is left looking at results for “ca”.
steps.picture: After. Page shows, no check. Both start. nothing. “cat” lands. “cat”. “ca” lands. “ca”. stale.

steps.title: Answer: number each search, and publish only the latest
steps.line: Predict: “cat” lands first with ticket 2. Published or dropped?
steps.caption: Give each search a ticket from a counter as it starts: “ca” gets 1, “cat” gets 2, and latest is now 2. Finishing changes neither. When a result lands, publish it only if its ticket is still the latest. Starting a newer request makes every older ticket stale; arrival order cannot make an old ticket current again.
steps.picture: “ca”: ticket 1. “cat”: ticket 2. latest = 2. // when a search starts. const ticket = ++latest. // when its result lands. if (ticket === latest) publish(result).

steps.title: Answer: published. “cat” lands with ticket 2, the latest
steps.line: Predict: “ca” lands next with ticket 1. Published or dropped?
steps.caption: “cat” carries ticket 2 and latest is 2, so the guard publishes its results. Both rules now show “cat”.
steps.picture: “cat”: ticket 2. latest = 2. =. Publish “cat”. if (ticket === latest).   publish(result).

steps.title: Answer: dropped. “ca” lands with ticket 1, not the latest 2
steps.line: Latest is still 2: finishing a search does not change it.
steps.caption: “ca” carries ticket 1 and latest is 2, so the guard drops its results. Without the guard the page would now show “ca”; with it, the page shows “cat”.
steps.picture: “ca”: ticket 1. latest = 2. ≠. Drop “ca”. if (ticket === latest).   publish(result).

steps.title: With the guard the page ends on “cat”; without it, on “ca”
steps.line: Both searches have finished; the user still wants “cat”.
steps.caption: Without the guard, the page ends on “ca”; with it, on “cat”. Older “ca” lands last and would overwrite “cat”; its ticket is stale, so the guard drops it. The guard drops stale results without cancelling the old search, which still runs to the end.
steps.picture: After. No guard. Guard on. Both start. nothing. nothing. “cat” lands. “cat”. “cat”. “ca” lands. “ca”. “cat”.
